gist: Manx shearwaters experience jet lag during long foraging trips over the ocean.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A study published in Science revealed that Manx shearwaters get jet-lagged when flying across time zones on foraging trips. Because they navigate using the Sun and their internal clocks fall out of sync with local time, they veer slightly off course.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The navigational errors reach up to around 15 degrees, adding only a few extra kilometres to their journeys. Understanding how birds manage this could help researchers design bio-inspired autonomous navigation systems and potentially offer insights into mitigating jet lag in humans.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Scientists plan to investigate whether these time shifts affect foraging timing, food delivery, breeding success, and whether other animals routinely experience similar jet lag.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The FDA proposed withdrawing Tavneos approval due to alleged study data manipulation by ChemoCentryx. Whistleblowers and a lawsuit revealed that trial data had been unblinded and re-adjudicated to secure approval. While the European Union and the United Kingdom pulled the product, Amgen maintained that the drug works and defended its availability.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The case raises serious questions about drug approval safeguards, scientific integrity, and the reliance on pivotal trials conducted by small companies. Experts warn that lacking rigorous oversight leaves patients and physicians in a state of uncertainty.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: A court hearing is expected to consider a proposed lawsuit settlement, while the FDA follows a legal stepwise approach toward potential drug withdrawal. Amgen plans to present new data at a November conference and may sue the agency.
